beats.narration_text: Ciao. This is Liam, in for Bear, with a short film for INFO seventy-three seventy-five, Computational Skepticism for AI. You might ask what kind of person should supervise an AI. The chapter says that is the wrong question. Not personality traits, not vibes. The question is what a supervisor can do that the system cannot do for itself.

show.event: types 'To supervise an AI, what kind of person do you need?'
backspaces 'kind of person do you need' -> 'must you do that it can't do for itself' on the spoken correction

beats.motion_claim: The writer types the naive question (what kind of person supervises an AI) and corrects it to the real one (what must you do that it can't do for itself).

beats.narration_text: Four terms. Capacity: something the supervisor can do that the system cannot do for itself. Prior: the sense, built over years, of what kinds of cases tend to be what kinds of cases. Formulation: the exact question the system is being asked to answer. And integration: many outputs made into one decision that someone stands behind.

beats.narration_text: Verification is the problem. A model makes an output, and someone has to check it against the world. That someone is the supervisor, standing between the model and the world. The chapter counts five things the supervisor does there that the model cannot do for itself.

shot.visual_intent: The dark model block arrives on the left ('model') and a white output slip pops out of it; the supervisor peg rises in the middle ('supervisor'); the patient peg on a kraft chair fades in on the right ('the world'); the slip slides from the model to the supervisor; five small kraft tiles rise in a row above the supervisor with ink numerals 1 to 5.

five tiles rise above the supervisor

beats.narration_text: One. Plausibility auditing. The chapter's case: a low triage score for a forty-nine-year-old with a swollen leg. An experienced clinician looks at it, and something twitches. The twitch is the audit: a check against a prior, the sense built over years of what kinds of cases tend to be what.

shot.visual_intent: The slip ('low score') slides from the model to the supervisor; the patient sits on the chair with a terracotta dot on the leg; behind the supervisor a stack of pages rises ('prior'); the supervisor peg twitches, a small rock left and right, and an ink question mark pops up above it.

show.event: the prior stack rises behind the supervisor

beats.narration_text: The model cannot do this for itself. It has its training data. The supervisor has the world. When nobody audits, the failure is quiet: the score arrives in a credible format, nobody asks whether it makes sense on its face, and it goes through.

shot.visual_intent: A kraft crate rises beside the model ('training data'); a line arcs from the supervisor to the patient ('the world'); then, with the supervisor idle, the slip slides straight past the supervisor to the patient and an ink check lands on it ('credible format').

show.event: the supervisor's line to the world
the slip goes straight through; a check lands

shot.motion_claim: A kraft crate rises beside the model ('training data'); a line arcs from the supervisor to the patient ('the world'); then, with the supervisor idle, the slip slides straight past the supervisor to the patient and an ink check lands on it ('credible format').

beats.narration_text: Two. Problem formulation. The chapter says most AI failures are failures of formulation, not performance. The triage system answered: what statistical category is this presentation? The clinical question was: how likely is a life-threatening condition? The first was answered well. The second was never asked.

shot.visual_intent: Two question slips beside the supervisor: 'category?' slides into the model and an answered slip pops out with an ink check; 'life-threatening?' starts toward the model and stops short, and the label 'never asked' lands beside it.

show.event: the first goes in and is answered
the second stops short: never asked

beats.narration_text: Three. Tool orchestration. AI is one tool among many. For each sub-problem, the supervisor picks the tool: the AI, human judgment, a different model, or, the hardest call, no tool yet: we do not know how to do this well enough to deploy.

shot.visual_intent: Four kraft plinths in a row: the dark model block ('AI'), a plain peg ('human'), a lighter second model block, and an empty plinth ('no tool yet'); the supervisor's cursor sweeps along the row, each object swells under it, and it lands on the empty plinth, which gets a terracotta dot.

show.event: it lands on no tool yet

shot.motion_claim: Four kraft plinths in a row: the dark model block ('AI'), a plain peg ('human'), a lighter second model block, and an empty plinth ('no tool yet'); the supervisor's cursor sweeps along the row, each object swells under it, and it lands on the empty plinth, which gets a terracotta dot.

beats.narration_text: Saying we should not deploy this here is supervisory work, and often the most valuable work the supervisor does. The failure runs the other way: AI used because it is available, not because it is right for the task, because nobody has the mandate to say no.

shot.visual_intent: The AI block on the left, a sub-problem slip on a plinth on the right; the supervisor draws an ink cross on the path between them ('not here'); then the supervisor and the cross fade, and the AI block slides onto the sub-problem by itself ('available').

beats.narration_text: Four. Interpretive judgment. The chapter's example: a five percent false-positive rate is fine for a spam filter, and catastrophic for a cancer screen. The same number, two meanings. The number is not the meaning; the meaning is the number in the domain. The failure: numbers read off a dashboard with no domain translation.

shot.visual_intent: The supervisor holds a slip with one ink hero number, 5%, captioned 'the chapter's example'; a kraft crate on the left ('spam filter') and the patient on the chair on the right ('cancer screen'); a copy of the slip slides to the crate and an ink check lands; another slides to the patient and an ink cross lands.

show.event: to the spam filter: a check
to the cancer screen: a cross

beats.narration_text: Five. Executive integration. Outputs from many tools, many models and many people, synthesized into one decision that someone stands behind. Somewhere in the organization, the buck has to stop. If there is no such place, the system has no decision-maker, only outputs.

shot.visual_intent: Three sources across the top: the model block, the lighter second model, and a plain peg; each emits a slip; the slips converge on the supervisor standing on a kraft plinth in the middle; one decision slip lands in front with a terracotta seal ('decision', 'buck stops').

show.event: they converge on the supervisor's plinth

shot.motion_claim: Three sources across the top: the model block, the lighter second model, and a plain peg; each emits a slip; the slips converge on the supervisor standing on a kraft plinth in the middle; one decision slip lands in front with a terracotta seal ('decision', 'buck stops').

beats.narration_text: The chapter calls this the rarest capacity, and the one most often missing from AI deployments, because no model produces it and most pipelines have no place for it. The failure: the pipeline produces decisions nobody owns, and when something goes wrong, accountability dissolves into the architecture.

shot.visual_intent: The same three sources; the plinth and the supervisor are gone; the three slips converge on the empty middle and pile up with no seal ('no owner'); then the pile slides apart, one slip back under each source, and the middle is empty again.

the pile slides apart: accountability dissolves

beats.narration_text: These five are vocabulary for now. By the end of the book, you can look at any deployment and name, for each step, which capacity is exercised and by whom. Where you cannot name it, you have found a gap. And in the chapter's words: gaps are where the patients die.

shot.visual_intent: The five tiles from the opening, now five kraft plinths in a row with ink numerals 1 to 5; a small supervisor peg pops onto plinths one, two, three and five ('by whom'); plinth four stays empty and the label 'gap' lands over it; the patient on the chair slides in beneath the empty plinth.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Pick one AI deployment you know, or one step of one, and paste this into Claude: Here is one AI deployment I know, or one step of it: describe it. For each of the five supervisory capacities, plausibility auditing, problem formulation, tool orchestration, interpretive judgment and executive integration, write who exercises it, in one line each, or write nobody. Then tell me which line you are least sure of, and why. Then check two things yourself. Is every who a named role, not the team? And did you write nobody at least once, honestly?
